question: Prepare an evidence brief for sertraline during lactation using the medication evidence brief tool. Include questions to ask my clinician, source links, and missing evidence limitations. Do not provide medication decisions or doses.
criteria: Honor the question, source provenance, visible gaps and three distinct axes. No dosing or personal treatment decision. Questions for a clinician are preparation, not source-authored evidence.
answer:
## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Evidence status:** Sertraline was exactly identified as the single ingredient sertraline. The retrieved material is partial and does not determine an individual treatment plan. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports that a midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported in that passage. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one reported case, a mother reported increased milk supply during a one-week interruption and decreased supply after restarting sertraline. The returned extract does not establish the exact timing of other relevant events or prove causation. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed also reports discussion of galactorrhea and a pharmacovigilance analysis concerning hyperprolactinemia. The complete supporting passages were not returned. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are source-reported observations, not proof that sertraline caused the effects.

### Measured exposure in milk

The returned LactMed extract reported these milk concentrations:

- **Sertraline:** mean **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, from a pooled analysis involving 15 mothers. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- **Sertraline:** mean **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; **norsertraline:** mean **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1,498 mcg/L**, in a study with extensive milk and maternal-serum sampling over 24 hours. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- At two months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline in four mothers sampled at random times. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a report involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline; the returned passage does not provide a complete infant-exposure description. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

**Infant-level information:** No infant-level concentration excerpt was returned. Infant specimen type and the complete infant-level measurement record are therefore missing from this extract. Milk concentrations are research measurements, not dose instructions.

### Observed infant outcomes

- One report described benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in a four-month-old infant and agitation that reportedly resolved spontaneously. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate group of 26 infants, the returned passage reported no detectable acute adverse reactions to sertraline in breast milk. The returned summary does not provide the complete study context. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 14 mothers and their breastfed infants, whole-blood serotonin measurements were obtained after maternal therapy. The passage reports infant serotonin averages before and after therapy and the authors’ interpretation concerning platelet serotonin uptake. This is an observed laboratory finding from that study, not an individual prediction. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The retrieved extract includes additional infant-outcome material, but the **Effects in Breastfed Infants** section was truncated. The underlying study count and complete study designs were not established from this extract. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### FAERS report-only context

The FDA spontaneous-report query returned these top terms and counts:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

The query covered reports matching sertraline in an **any-population report subset**, not a confirmed lactation or infant cohort. These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; they do not establish causation and lack exposure denominators. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Label context

The selected DailyMed product was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**. The retrieved label included a standalone **“8.2 Lactation”** entry, but the tool identified a title/code mismatch requiring verification. The lactation section was not truncated; the pregnancy section was truncated. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The retrieved medicine-taker section listed adverse reactions and warnings including hypersensitivity reactions, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, activation of mania/hypomania, discontinuation syndrome, seizures, angle-closure glaucoma, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction. Other expected adult warning sections were missing from the returned extract; that is an extraction limitation, not evidence that the full label lacks them. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Literature-retrieval limitations

The search was bounded and returned five PubMed records; it was not a systematic review. Abstract text was retrieved for **3 of 5** requested records. No abstract text was returned for **PMID 38133585** or **PMID 32320387**. No records were unreturned, and no abstract lookups failed. Missing abstracts are retrieval limitations, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. Titles alone were not used to describe outcomes. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the returned extract. The brief therefore cannot establish the complete evidence base, complete infant-level exposure data, or the full context of all reported outcomes. [S54](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Questions to ask your clinician

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact product, formulation, and all active ingredients?
2. How closely do these study populations match my lactation context and my infant’s age or prematurity?
3. Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
4. How should the reported milk-supply observations be interpreted in the context of my underlying condition and other factors affecting lactation?
5. What uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?
6. What benefits, risks, and follow-up questions should we address together?

evidence_axes.label: Effect on the pregnant or lactating person

items.text: Sertraline has caused galactorrhea in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients, sometimes with normal serum prolactin.[47-53] However, in a study of cases of hyperprolactinemia and its symptoms (e.g., gynecomastia) reported to a French pharmacovigilance center, sertraline was not found to have an increased risk of causing hyperprolactinemia compared to other drugs.[54] The prolactin level in a mother with established lactation may not affect her ability to breastfeed.

evidence_axes.label: Measured transfer or exposure to fetus or infant

items.text: Sertraline is metabolized to norsertraline (desmethylsertraline), which has antidepressant activity of about 10% that of sertraline.

In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 4 unpublished cases, the authors found that 15 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 83 mg (range 25 to 200 mg) had an average breastmilk sertraline level of 45 mcg/L (range 7 to 207 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of sertraline.

Twenty-six women who were an average of 15.8 weeks postpartum (range 5 to 36 weeks) and receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied while breastfeeding with extensive milk and serum sampling over a 24-hour period.
All milk samples had detectable sertraline (average 129 mcg/L; range 11 to 938 mcg/L) and norsertraline (average 258 mcg/L; range 20 to 1498 mcg/L).

result.answer_rules: Use for explicit requests to prepare an evidence brief for pregnancy, breastfeeding or a child's medicine (population neonate, infant, child, adolescent or pediatric). Pediatric briefs use three pediatric axes: effectiveness and safety findings, pharmacokinetics and exposure, and labeling status and changes (DailyMed 8.4, FDA pediatric labeling changes, BPCA/PTN links), plus off_label_context on where adult and off-label evidence is documented. Pregnancy and lactation briefs include research_priorities_context with the 15 PRGLAC recommendations. Call before optional individual source lookups when preflight requested_workflow requires it. Compile public evidence and questions to ask a clinician, never a safety verdict. Normalize the exact product then search EACH confirmed active ingredient. Keep ingredient evidence separate; combined effects and interactions are not established. Preserve requested age band, source ages, missing evidence, dose flags and pregnancy limits. Also the tool for focused parent questions about side effects in the person taking the medicine versus findings in a breastfed infant: the label's medicine_taker_sections and the LactMed infant findings are both returned, and must be kept apart. Includes literature metadata and abstract_coverage. Disclose missing abstract text, unreturned records and retrieval failures; preserve required_display_notices. Metadata and titles alone cannot support study-outcome claims. Display FAERS report_only_context separately, even when observed-outcome rows are empty. Report counts are unconfirmed signals, not established outcomes. detail='summary' (default) returns every axis with totals, the first passages per list and compact source records; say that it is a summary and never present it as complete. Use detail='full' for every passage and the source text.
